results.summary_before: This project is a two-player scoreboard controlled by two pushbuttons. It counts points for each player, with short presses incrementing and long presses decrementing the score. The scores are displayed on two 7-segment displays that alternate between showing 'P1' or 'P2' and the respective score. The design includes debounce logic and was tested with testbenches.

results.summary_before: This is a digital traffic light controller with pedestrian request handling and MAX7219 display interface. It controls car and pedestrian lights with precise timing, button debouncing, and a countdown displayed on LED matrices. The design includes an FSM, clock divider, MAX7219 driver, and SPI master, and was validated in simulation and Wokwi. It requires external LEDs, pushbuttons, and MAX7219 modules.

results.summary_before: This design renders an analog-style clock on a VGA monitor, using a CORDIC algorithm to compute hand angles and pixel positions. It includes an alarm function that compares a set alarm time to the current time and outputs a 3.15 kHz square wave pulsed at 1 Hz for a buzzer. Time and alarm settings are adjusted via five external pushbuttons, and the VGA output follows the standard Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD pinout. The design requires a 31.5 MHz clock and external pushbuttons with pulldown resistors, and the alarm output needs an external driver for a buzzer.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design implements a memory built-in self-test (MBIST) controller with built-in self-repair (MBISR) for an embedded 256x8-bit SRAM. It uses the March C- algorithm to detect faults and can remap faulty addresses using CAM-based repair, providing DONE and FAIL status outputs. The system automatically tests and repairs the memory on-the-fly, making it suitable for reliable memory subsystems. The documentation is limited to a brief description, with no external testing details or results provided.

results.summary_before: This SystemVerilog project is a digital recreation of the MOS6581 SID sound chip, supporting most of its original features. It is configured via a 4-wire SPI interface and outputs a 1-bit PDM audio signal at 10 MHz. To use it, one connects an SPI master and a low-pass reconstruction filter to the PDM output, then programs voices using registers to generate tones. The design includes a CocoTB test suite and is notable for bringing a classic synthesizer chip to Tiny Tapeout.

results.summary_before: This is a maze exploration game rendered on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED display over I2C, with the player navigating a 16x8 hardcoded maze from start to goal. The core game logic is a combinational circuit generated from DSLX and wrapped in Verilog holding 123 bits of state, with up to two walls breakable and audio feedback through a piezo speaker. It requires an OLED, a piezo speaker, eight pushbuttons, and 4.7k pull-up resistors on the I2C lines. Buttons are synchronized and debounced, and the I2C runs at about 195 kHz using pseudo open-drain bidirectional pins.
